signals.rawAbstract: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings. Here's a quick demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BFfbXAwRq98 Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman. I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. literacy.plainFullTitle: Free, Private, Open-Source Meeting Transcription App Yogurt

1.analogy: Think of it like a personal scribe who listens to your meetings, takes notes, and summarizes them without ever leaving your side or sharing them with anyone else.
1.everydayWhy: This app helps busy professionals manage their meeting notes more privately and efficiently, without the need for cloud services or third-party accounts.

2.whatHappened: Eric built Yogurt, a free, open-source desktop app that transcribes, summarizes, and chats about your meetings using on-device AI models.
2.whoBuiltIt: Eric, a developer, built Yogurt in his free time.
2.problemSolved: Yogurt addresses the need for a private, cost-effective solution for managing meeting notes and summaries, without the risks associated with cloud services.

3.bridgeSummary: Yogurt uses on-device AI models to transcribe and summarize meetings, leveraging techniques like MCP (Model Composition Protocol) and Open-Weights for efficient model management, and LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) for fine-tuning summaries.

4.roiAndFinOps: By keeping the data on the user's device, Yogurt reduces costs and enhances privacy, making it a cost-effective solution for managing meeting notes. It also streamlines the workflow by eliminating the need for cloud services.
4.readinessAndRisk: Yogurt is currently in a beta stage, with a focus on GA production readiness. It requires careful sandboxing and compliance checks to ensure it meets banking industry standards.
4.clientAdvice: BANKING leadership should consider a pilot program to evaluate Yogurt's performance and security before full deployment, ensuring strict compliance and data protection measures are in place.

5.architectureBrief: Yogurt employs on-device AI models and techniques like MCP for model composition and Open-Weights for efficient model management, with LoRA used for fine-tuning summaries. It uses a local MCP server for sharing summaries with third-party services like Anthropic or OpenAI.
5.specsAndCaveats: Yogurt's performance is dependent on the computational resources of the user's device. It may face challenges with large-scale deployments due to varying device capabilities. The app's security and privacy features are robust but require ongoing validation and updates.
5.streetConsensus: The community is excited about Yogurt's potential but is awaiting more detailed validation and real-world testing to confirm its reliability and security.

streetQuotes.text: I built Axe because I got tired of every AI tool trying to be a chatbot.

signals.rawAbstract: I built Axe because I got tired of every AI tool trying to be a chatbot. Most frameworks want a long-lived session with a massive context window doing everything at once. That's expensive, slow, and fragile. Good software is small, focused, and composable... AI agents should be too. Axe treats LLM agents like Unix programs. Each agent is a TOML config with a focused job. Such as code reviewer, log analyzer, commit message writer. You can run them from the CLI, pipe data in, get results out. You can use pipes to chain them together. Or trigger from cron, git hooks, CI. What Axe is: - 12MB binary, two dependencies. no framework, no Python, no Docker (unless you want it) - Stdin piping, something like `git diff | axe run reviewer` just works - Sub-agent delegation. Where agents call other agents via tool use, depth-limited - Persistent memory. If you want, agents can remember across runs without you managing state - MCP support. Axe can connect any MCP server to your agents - Built-in tools. Such as web_search and url_fetch out of the box - Multi-provider. Bring what you love to use.. Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, or anything in models.dev format - Path-sandboxed file ops. Keeps agents locked to a working directory Written in Go. No daemon, no GUI. What would you automate first?

literacy.plainFullTitle: A 12MB Binary Replacing AI Frameworks for Specific Tasks

1.analogy: Think of it like a set of specialized tools in a toolbox, each designed for a specific job, rather than a single all-purpose tool that tries to do everything.
1.everydayWhy: These tools help banks automate specific tasks more efficiently, like reviewing code or generating commit messages, without the overhead of a full AI framework.

2.whatHappened: A developer built Axe, a 12MB binary, to replace AI frameworks by focusing on specific tasks like code review or log analysis.
2.whoBuiltIt: The developer built Axe, a tool designed to replace AI frameworks with smaller, focused agents.
2.problemSolved: The problem addressed is the inefficiency and fragility of AI frameworks that require long-lived sessions and massive context windows, which are expensive and slow.

3.bridgeSummary: Axe treats AI agents like Unix programs, where each agent is a TOML config with a specific job, and can be run from the CLI, piped together, or triggered by cron or git hooks. It uses MCP (Model as a Code Provider) support to connect to various AI models and provides built-in tools like web_search and url_fetch.

4.roiAndFinOps: By automating specific tasks, Axe can significantly reduce operational costs and improve workflow efficiency, making it a cost-effective solution for banks looking to automate repetitive tasks.
4.readinessAndRisk: Axe is production-ready with a small binary size and no dependencies on Python or Docker, but banks should consider sandboxing and compliance risks, especially when integrating with external AI models.
4.clientAdvice: Banks should pilot Axe with a few specific tasks to evaluate its effectiveness before wider deployment, ensuring proper sandboxing and compliance checks.

5.architectureBrief: Axe is built in Go, with a persistent memory feature that allows agents to remember state across runs, and supports sub-agent delegation via tool use. It connects to various AI models through MCP support and provides built-in tools like web_search and url_fetch.
5.specsAndCaveats: Axe has a 12MB binary size with two dependencies, supports multiple AI providers, and uses stdin piping for efficient data flow. It addresses potential failure modes by sandboxing file operations and limiting sub-agent depth.
5.streetConsensus: The community is excited about Axe's potential to simplify AI integration, but concerns about sandboxing and compliance risks need to be addressed before widespread adoption.

Open-Weights means the trained AI brain files are publicly downloadable so organizations can run them privately on their own hardware with zero data leaving the building.
A Context Window is how much text, code, or video an AI can hold in its head during a single conversation before older details start dropping out.
Agentic Tool Use means the AI does more than chat—it plans multi-step tasks, runs terminal commands, edits files, and calls software tools on your behalf.

signals.rawAbstract: It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org! Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila! HackerTube: Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3. EDIT : A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

The transcript from the event is a bit noisy, so I wanted to write up the main intellectual content in a cleaner form. The short version is that I think we have crossed a new threshold. LLMs are no longer just chatbots or autocomplete. They are becoming a new programmable layer for digital work. This is the compact version of the conversation. 1. December 2025 Was an Agentic Inflection Point I said recently that I have never felt more behind as a programmer. The reason is not that programming became harder in the old sense. It is that the default workflow changed. For much of 2025, tools like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor-like agents were useful but still required frequent correction. Around December 2025, I felt a step change: the generated chunks got larger, more coherent, and more reliable. I started trusting the agents with more of the work. The unit of programming changed from typing lines of code to delegating larger "macro actions": Implement this feature. Refactor this subsystem. Research this library. Set up this service. Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. signals.rawAbstract: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn; That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT. Via Lobste.rs Tags: mysql, postgresql,

signals.rawAbstract: Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven't read it, you can get a copy here. I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1, and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic's newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I'll go with: "an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer." This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where "using a computer" is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is "almost" AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: "I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this." Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The "G" in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? To test that, I gave the AI a variety of hard challenges in different domains: Hack some hardware from a single prompt: I have a tiny USB keyboard with a few light-up keys on my desk called a Codex Micro (ironically built to work with ChatGPT), and I asked Fable to turn it into a game console. signals.rawAbstract: My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence, I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence, I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single "orchestrator" agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn't have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad ("make it better"). It even caught that I'd gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post "28 months on the exponential." Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. "This is the worst AI you will ever use" I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence, and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. We are living in an exponential The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. From the release of GPT-4 to the end of the METR measure, the amount of work AI could do doubled eight times. In 2024, an AI could do a four minute task. At the moment I turned in my draft of Co-Existence in April of 2026, an AI could do 17 hours of human work. And then the benchmark ran out. signals.rawAbstract: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova, COO of Linear, about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation. We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. Jump to the MCP discussion → "Issue tracking is dead" When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. signals.rawAbstract: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia's profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia's business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia's number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen's more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides, recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto "ownership of intelligence" and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there's little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek's DeepInfer release, they're far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy. Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen's support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out. Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models. There's a major swell in Democratic government funding towards candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering "safety". Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. signals.rawAbstract: Our first open model economy research note for paid subscribers. My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents. For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume. Thankfully, Google releases token volumes for the entire platform and API usage in their earnings reports. signals.rawAbstract: Harness Design Patterns Pattern 1: Workflow Automation The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965), where he defined an "ultraintelligent machine" as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase "recursive self-improvement" for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system, which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic; OpenAI ). I explicitly mention "deployment system" because the layer between the raw model and the real-world context seems to be as important as the model's raw intelligence (i.e. the evals right after pretraining). Harnesses are important components of AI deployment, as shown by successful coding agent products such as Claude Code and Codex. A harness is the system surrounding a base model that orchestrates execution and decides how the model thinks and plans, calls tools and acts, perceives and manages context, stores artifacts, and evaluates results. This one post will focus on research around harness engineering and how it contributes to RSI. Much recent work on auto-research, self-improving agents, and evolutionary program search can be organized around this question. Other work on model self-play, synthetic data, test-time training and a broader theme of continual learning also matches the RSI vision (e.g. Yuan et al. 2024, Chen et al. 2024 ), Zhao et al. 2025, Choi et al. 2026 )) but they will not be the focus of this post. Compared with early agent frameworks, "agent = LLM + memory + tools + planning + action", harnesses engineering additionally include workflow design (e.g. loop engineering), evaluation, permission controls, and persistent state management. It is no longer only prompt templates, but closer to runtime and software system design: how the model observes, acts, memorizes, checks itself, and improves. The design should be deliberately simple and generic to enable generalization, likely with reference to existing software engineering practices to benefit from prertaining knowlege. There is also a strong analogy between operating systems and harnesses. Similar to an OS, a harness should encapsulate complicated logic while keeping the interface simple. Meanwhile, configs, tool interfaces and other protocols may gradually become standardized across the industry. Defining a workflow in which the model can operate, test, and iterate is a key design for automation. Karpathy's autoresearch repo ( https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch ) is a clean example of how such a workflow can be constructed. signals.rawAbstract: Scaling Laws in Data-Infinite Region Kaplan et al.'s Scaling Laws Chinchilla Scaling Laws Method 1: Fix model sizes, vary the token budget Trickiness of Fitting Scaling Laws in Reality Toy simulation Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$. This predictability makes scaling laws highly valuable in practice. A common workflow is to fit scaling laws on a handful of small runs and then extrapolate to estimate the token and compute requirements for larger models. The predictability of generalization error with scale had already been investigated before scaling laws became a mainstream concept. Amari et al. (1992) derived four types of learning curves using a Bayesian approach and the annealed approximation. Deterministic learning algorithm, noiseless data, one unique solution: $\epsilon \sim c \cdot D^{-1}$, where $c$ is some constant. Deterministic learning algorithm, noiseless data, multiple equivalent solutions: $\epsilon \sim c \cdot D^{-2}$; the learning is faster with each new data point, because the model only learns the optimal manifold of parameters, instead of finding the single solution point. Deterministic learning algorithm, noisy data: $\epsilon \sim c \cdot D^{-1/2}$; noises in data make learning harder. Stochastic learning algorithm, noisy data: $\epsilon \sim c \cdot D^{-1} + E$; here the irreducible loss $E$ is the residual error that a stochastic learner cannot reduce further, for example when the model runs out of capacity on large data. All four types of learning curves follow a power law: where $E$ can be 0 and $\alpha = -2, -1, -1/2$. Although their theoretical setup is based on a simplified binary classification task, it points in a useful direction for building empirical ML loss prediction models.

signals.rawAbstract: Learn how OpenAI built the Performance Factory, a system of Codex-powered workflows that finds and fixes performance issues to help keep ChatGPT fast. Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues. By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap. In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day. Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production. As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains. Software work evolves from manual labor to partnering with machines to agent factories. 1. Pre-Codex. Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools. 2. Codex as a partner. Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

signals.rawAbstract: Our previous post in this series introduced the Ranking Engineer Agent (REA), an autonomous system that generates hypotheses, designs experiments, and proves new machine learning (ML) techniques on ads ranking models. Now, we’re sharing how we propagate ranking model improvements like architectural advancements and training optimizations efficiently across a large and diverse fleet of ads ranking models. This post walks through this process that we call “technique propagation” and how we’re optimizing the process using AI agents. Since agents began driving execution in March 2026, we estimate AI agents handle over 60% of all technique propagation. Measured against the same work before agents, early results show 3x greater engineering productivity, a median 4x reduction in training compute across select combinations, and an estimated $45M+ in compute savings by the end of the year. Meta's ads recommendation system is powered by a large number of distinct ads ranking models, each serving different product surfaces and advertiser objectives, and each with its own architecture, training data, and serving constraints. Across this portfolio, ML researchers and engineers are continuously advancing the state-of-the-art through innovations we call "techniques.” A technique is anything that makes a ranking model better such as architectural advancements like Wukong factorization layers, Interformer interaction networks, richer data representations, training optimizations, or efficiency improvements in training and inference. However, because each model has its own architecture, data, and training and serving constraints, a technique proven on one model almost never copy-pastes onto the next. At the same time, speed matters because ML techniques have a shelf life. An innovation that delivers gains today may be superseded within a couple of model development cycles. The faster proven techniques reach the full model fleet, the more value they deliver before the next generation of techniques arrive. So how do we propagate a technique to a diverse fleet of models as quickly as possible, while minimizing engineering bandwidth and compute? Scaling Technique Propagation Propagating a growing inventory of proven techniques across a large fleet of diverse models creates a combinatorially expanding space of technique-model combinations to explore, where both engineering bandwidth and compute become significant constraints. The standard way to adapt a technique is to have engineers who are domain experts manually execute adaptation. An engineer studies how a technique interacts with a specific model's architecture, generalizes it, and tunes it to that model's constraints. This produces the strongest results, and is still the process for our highest-revenue models, but it does not scale to all of the models in the space. Each adaptation is effort-intensive and demands deep familiarity with both the technique and the target model. So throughput is capped by engineering bandwidth while the opportunity for adaptation grows much faster. The second constraint on propagation is compute. signals.rawAbstract: As ML ecosystems grow to a large number of production models, the bottleneck is no longer inventing new techniques to improve these models, but rather shipping them reliably and efficiently across a fragmented model space, creating a rising tide that lifts all the boats. At Meta, we built a template-driven approach that standardizes model design into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, turning model iteration from a per-model problem into a shared systems problem. Over the last two years, this approach reduced per-model engineering time by 92%, shipped 5000+ technique-model combinations, improved offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift covering 70% of models by count. This work is fully detailed in our paper, “ Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Template-Driven ML Development for Large Model Ecosystems.” Meta’s ads ranking systems process billions of daily requests across a diverse array of products and optimization goals, served by a large number of production models. At that scale, the main challenge in improving user relevance and advertiser value has shifted from inventing new techniques to propagating them. Every high-impact idea needs to reach every model it applies to, and adapting it one model at a time does not scale with the fleet. Fragmentation compounds quickly in large-scale ML systems. A new architecture lands on one model, but bringing it to every corner of the ecosystem may take years. A platform migration works for one family of models, but breaks on a long tail of specialized configurations. A tuning insight improves one model, but says little about the next one because the underlying setup is too different. Over time, propagation becomes more difficult than the innovation itself. Meta's ads ranking ecosystem ran into this exact problem. As the number of production models grew with the diversity of ads optimization objectives, so did the diversity of architectures, features, training settings, serving constraints, and platform-specific logic. That diversity gave teams flexibility, but it also created three systemic problems: high engineering cost to ship new ideas broadly, high reliability cost from an explosion of corner cases, and low predictability when trying to estimate the ecosystem-wide impact of a change. The deeper issue is that fragmentation creates an unfavorable scaling law for engineering itself. If each idea must be evaluated and adapted per model, the work grows linearly with the number of models. That is manageable early on, but becomes a serious bottleneck when you have a large number of models. Fragmentation also weakens automation. AutoML and optimization systems work best in a structured space, but when every model has a different shape, the highest-potential techniques reach only a subset of models. Our answer was not to add another layer of automation on top of this complexity. Instead, we started by reducing the complexity itself. signals.rawAbstract: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

signals.title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis

divergence.summary: Balanced signal (49 hype / 52 street) — validate on domain workload before broad rollout.

streetQuotes.author: HF Daily Papers
streetQuotes.text: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame.

signals.rawAbstract: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. signals.rawAbstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

signals.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience

divergence.summary: Balanced signal (56 hype / 50 street) — validate on domain workload before broad rollout.

streetQuotes.author: arXiv
streetQuotes.text: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging.

signals.rawAbstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

signals.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming

signals.rawAbstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

signals.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning

divergence.summary: Balanced signal (49 hype / 52 street) — validate on domain workload before broad rollout.

streetQuotes.author: arXiv
streetQuotes.text: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes.

signals.rawAbstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

signals.rawAbstract: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

signals.rawAbstract: Hey HN, this is Andy from Respan ( https://www.respan.ai ). We are building an open-source Rust AI gateway. It is a decoupled gateway, so everything is a plugin, including different providers, protocols (MCP, voice), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features (fallbacks, PII redaction, smart routing). Instead of packaging tons of providers and features into one gateway, Respan provides a small core and public interfaces that teams can use to assemble the AI infrastructure their application needs. That way, users can build their own features as additional plugins without having to change the gateway's core. Here’s a video demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVv2ibXiTXM There are countless LLM gateways and most of them solve a common problem: calling different providers from a single endpoint. However, adding new features can become prohibitively difficult. So developers can end up building another gateway to solve a specific problem. We've been building our gateway based on LiteLLM since 2024, and now it's providing services for thousands of orgs. Each org needs different API key settings, routes, and limits. To support that, we kept wrapping LiteLLM, adding more features to it, and at one stage, our wrapper code exceeded 100,000 lines. signals.rawAbstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. signals.rawAbstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp

divergence.summary: Balanced signal (53 hype / 59 street) — validate on domain workload before broad rollout.

streetQuotes.author: HF Daily Papers
streetQuotes.text: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale.

signals.rawAbstract: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community

signals.rawAbstract: I got tired of coding agents that feel like IDEs in disguise. Slow to start, full of chrome, opinionated about where you work. So I built one that doesn't get in the way. It's called *mini-coder*. The command is `mc`. Tagline: Small. Fast. Gets out of your way. Oh — and it mostly wrote itself (with some help from me). --- ## What it is mini-coder is a terminal-native AI coding agent built on *Bun.js* — fast startup, native TypeScript, built-in SQLite, no ceremony. It routes to *Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, and Zen* and auto-detects your provider from env vars. No config file to write. No account to create. No telemetry. Session memory lives in local SQLite. Resume your last session with `mc -c`, or pick one with `mc -r `. Your history stays on your machine. --- ## How it works The LLM gets a tight set of tools: `glob`, `grep`, `read`, `create`, `replace`, `insert`, `shell`, and `subagent`. That last one is the interesting bit — mini-coder can spawn parallel sub-agents for independent subtasks, up to 3 levels deep. It delegates, waits, synthesizes. It works the way you do. Inside the REPL, `!command` runs shell commands inline and `@file` references files with tab completion. Slash commands cover the essentials: `/model` to switch providers, `/plan` for read-only mode, `/ralph` for a fully autonomous loop, `/review`, `/undo`, `/new`, and `/help`. 16 ANSI colors only. I

5.architectureBrief: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem.
5.specsAndCaveats: We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset.
